title: Self-tracking selves and pervasive performing

(2026). Self-tracking selves and pervasive performing. In Power, M. (Ed.), Economy of Traces:Traceability, Tracking and the Accounts we Live By (pp. 215 - 252). Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/9780197681527.003.0008 Copy Share Abstract This chapter explores the relations between traceification, accounting, and self-formation. Accounts are formative by virtue of the “pull” by which the self encounters itself. Via digitized prosthetics for self-monitoring and self-accounting, enabled by social media and biosensors, the boundary between the organizational and notionally private sphere has become fluid. Three critical pathways of digital trace-enabled self-formation are discussed: profile construction and curation; the self as platform and social media-enabled feedback machine; and the self-tracking self, which pursues its “data-double”. These three themes reveal both the expanded and expanding reach of “performance” as a normative category, which demands monitoring and improvement across time, and how tracking is becoming valued as an end in itself. There is also a politics of traceability generated by the tension between the need for visibility and feedback (i.e. to know “how am I doing?”), and counter-values emphasizing privacy. Overall, the postulated shift in the accounts we live by towards tracking is correlated with formative processes that de-centre and dividuate the self.
